Management and Outcomes

Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Select appropriate surgical approaches that can be used for the management of various
acetabular fracture patterns.
Recognize the indications for surgical and nonsurgical management of acetabular fractures.
Identify the variables that contribute to successful management of acetabular fractures.
Review the expected short- and long-term outcomes of acetabular fractures.
Explain common complications that can occur after acetabular fracture management.
Background
Acetabular fractures are most commonly categorized according to the Judet and Letournel
classification system (Figure 1).

Most injuries result from a direct lateral impact to the hip or an axial load through the femur.
Maintenance of a stable, concentric hip joint is a primary goal of fracture management.
Surgical decision making is based on multiple factors, including the fracture pattern, articular
displacement, the extent of articular damage, congruency of the hip joint, and the physiologic
age and comorbidities of the patient.
Injury-related factors, such as neurological injury, damage to the blood supply of the femoral
head, and articular cartilage lesions of the acetabulum and femoral head, have been shown to
predict poor outcomes after management.
Accurate surgical reduction and stable fixation of the articular surface has been shown to
improve survivorship of the native hip after acetabular fracture.
Posttraumatic arthritis is the most common complication after acetabular fracture.
Conversion to total hip arthroplasty after acetabular fracture ranges from 8% to 35%.
Most conversions to hip arthroplasty occur within the first 2 years postinjury.1
Figure 1 Illustrations show the Letournel classification of acetabular fractures. (Reproduced from

Surgical Approaches
Multiple surgical approaches have been described for the surgical reduction and fixation of
acetabular fractures.
Selection of the most appropriate approach is based on the fracture pattern, associated soft-
tissue injury, and condition of the patient.
Some complex fracture patterns require the use of more than one approach.
The Kocher-Langenbeck and the Gibson approaches are commonly used to provide direct
access to the posterior aspect and indirect access to the anterior aspect of the acetabulum (
Figure 2).
The ilioinguinal and the anterior intrapelvic approaches are commonly used to provide direct
access to the anterior aspect and indirect access to the posterior aspect of the acetabulum. 
Surgical hip dislocation provides direct access to the posterior column, femoral head, and
articular surface of the entire acetabulum. Access to the anterior column is limited.
The extended iliofemoral approach provides access to the anterior and posterior columns via
the external surface of almost the entire innominate bone. It does not provide direct access to
the inside of the pelvis.

Kocher-Langenbeck Approach
Performed with the patient in the prone or lateral position (Video 1)
Most commonly used for the following fracture patterns:
Posterior wall
Posterior column
Transverse
Transverse and posterior wall
Posterior column and posterior wall
T-type
Superficial exposure splits the iliotibial band in combination with an intramuscular split of
gluteus maximus.

Deep exposure commonly requires tenotomy of the piriformis and the triceps coxae
(obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli).
Typical exposure affords direct visual and tactile access to the posterior column from the
cranial aspect of the ischial tuberosity to the greater sciatic notch.
Allows for indirect access via palpation of the anterior column and the quadrilateral surface
through the greater sciatic foramen
Video 1 Gorczyca JT, ed: Posterior Kocher-Langenbeck approach, in Selective Exposures in
Orthopaedic Surgery: The Pelvis [DVD]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2005.
Complications
Iatrogenic injury to the sciatic nerve
Hip extension and knee flexion decrease tension on the nerve.
Avoid pressure from retractor and reduction clamp placement.
Avoid placing multiple clamps and retractors in the greater and lesser sciatic notches at the
same time.
Recognize the variants of anatomy for the sciatic nerve.2

Heterotopic bone
Débridement of devitalized gluteal and triceps muscle may help decrease the incidence of
heterotopic ossification.3
Preoperative or postoperative radiation therapy can be used for prophylaxis in patients at
high risk for heterotopic ossification (head injury, burn injury, electrocution, prolonged
ventilation) but is not used routinely.4,5
Indomethacin prophylaxis has been shown to increase the rate of posterior wall and long
bone (femur) nonunion.6,7
Gibson Approach
Performed with the patient in the prone or lateral position
Used to provide increased exposure to the anterosuperior innominate bone and decrease the
risk of iatrogenic injury to the inferior gluteal nerve, which innervates the gluteus maximus
muscle
First described by Gibson as a modification of the Kocher-Langenbeck approach8
Can be used to manage acetabular fracture patterns managed via Kocher-Langenbeck
approach9
Differences between the Gibson and Kocher-Langenbeck approaches
Superficial surgical incision for the Gibson approach is made in line with the proximal
femoral shaft and continues straight to the iliac crest, dissimilar from the Kocher-Langenbeck
approach, which is angled or curved toward the posterior superior iliac spine from the tip of
the greater trochanter.
Interval between the gluteus maximus and the tensor fascia lata is used in the Gibson
approach; the Kocher-Langenbeck approach involves the use of a gluteus maximus split.
Similarities to Kocher-Langenbeck approach
Deep surgical retraction of gluteus medius muscle and release of the short external rotators
Placement of instruments and implants for fracture exposure, reduction, and fixation
Approach avoids superficial dissection through injured posterior tissues.
Can be combined with a trochanteric osteotomy, if necessary, to perform surgical hip
dislocation
Ilioinguinal Approach

Performed in with the patient in the supine position with longitudinal traction and the hip
flexed (Video 2)
Commonly used for the following fracture patterns:
Anterior wall
Anterior column
Transverse
Anterior plus posterior hemi-transverse
Associated both-column
Skin incision is from midline, just above pubic symphysis, to the posterior aspect of the iliac
crest
The first window (lateral window) is developed by releasing the external oblique muscle from
the iliac crest and elevating the iliacus muscle from the internal iliac fossa, which affords
access to the following:
Cranial and anterior aspect of the sacroiliac joint
Internal iliac fossa from the sacroiliac joint to the anterior superior iliac spine and the psoas
gutter
Cranial aspect of the posterior column
Quadrilateral surface from the pelvic brim to the ischial spine
The second window (middle window) is developed after the external oblique fascia is incised
and the floor of the inguinal canal is divided from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic
tubercle. The iliopectineal fascia separates the true pelvis from the false pelvis and needs to be
divided to complete the exposure of this window. The iliopectineal fascia divides the lacuna
musculorum laterally (iliopsoas muscle and femoral nerve) and the lacuna vasorum medially
(external iliac artery, vein, and lymphatics). After division and subsequent elevation of the
insertion of the iliopectineal fascia from the pectineal eminence, access to the following is
attained:
Pelvic brim and superior pubic ramus
Anterior wall
Quadrilateral surface
Posterior column
The third window (medial window) is developed via a vertical split of the rectus abdominis
muscles to gain access to the retropubic space of Retzius. Proper development of this window
exposes the pubic symphysis and enhances exposure of the following:
Bilateral superior pubic rami
True pelvis

Complications
Anastomoses between the internal and external iliac vessels should be identified and ligated
to avoid substantial bleeding (corona mortis).10
The lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator, sciatic, and femoral nerves are at risk for injury from
excessive retraction or reduction clamp placement.11
The external iliac artery and vein can be injured with retraction and clamp placement in the
second window.
Lymphatic injury from excessive dissection medial to the lacuna vasculorum may result in
ipsilateral lower extremity swelling.
Abdominal or inguinal hernia may result if the external oblique or inguinal ligament/canal are
not properly repaired.

Anterior Intrapelvic (Modified Stoppa) Approach
Performed with the patient in the supine position with the hip flexed; lateral traction can be
used if necessary (Video 3).
Originally described to manage injuries of the pelvic ring12
Indications for surgical approach expanded to manage some acetabular fractures.13-15
Commonly used for the following fracture patterns:
Anterior column
Transverse
Anterior plus posterior hemi-transverse
Associated both-column
A Pfannenstiel skin incision is made above the pubic symphysis, and a vertical midline split of
the rectus abdominus affords access to the retropubic space of Retzius.
Dissection is carried along the superior pubic ramus, releasing the iliopectineal fascia, and
posteriorly along the pelvic brim, elevating the iliacus muscle to the anterior aspect of the
sacroiliac joint to afford access to the lower third of the internal iliac fossa.
The obturator nerve is identified and mobilized so the obturator internus can be elevated,
exposing the quadrilateral surface and the medial aspect of the posterior column from the
ischial spine to the greater sciatic notch.
If access to the cranial aspect of the anterior column or the iliac crest is necessary, this
approach can be performed in combination with the first window of the ilioinguinal approach
or via an iliofemoral approach with or without an anterior superior iliac spine osteotomy.16,17

Surgical Hip Dislocation With Digastric Osteotomy
Performed with the patient in the lateral position, most often via the Gibson approach but can
be performed via the Kocher-Langenbeck approach
Allows for surgical access to the femoral head and the articular surface of the acetabulum19,20
Commonly used for the following patterns:
Concurrent femoral head and posterior wall acetabular fractures (Pipkin type IV)
Posterior wall
Transverse

Transverse and posterior wall
Posterior column and posterior wall
T-type
A digastric sliding trochanteric osteotomy is performed (gluteus medius and vastus lateralis
muscles remain attached to osteotomized trochanteric fragment).
A capsulotomy is performed to protect the terminal retinacular vessels and the ascending
cervical branches from the circumflex femoral arteries.
Flexion and external rotation of the hip allows for anterior dislocation of the femoral head.
Provides direct access to the posterior column; anterior, cranial, and posterior rim of
acetabulum; and the entire acetabular labrum
Allows for assessment of articular reduction and minimizes the risk of intra-articular
placement of fixation because the articular surface of the acetabulum is directly visualized
Complications: Same as with the Kocher-Langenbeck approach, with increased risk of the
following:
Trochanteric osteotomy malunion or nonunion, generally from poor fixation
Osteonecrosis— A capsulotomy that detaches the cranial and posterior capsule from the
area adjacent to the hip labrum and the acetabular rim best protects the ascending vessels.
Heterotopic ossification
Extended Iliofemoral Approach
Performed with the patient in the lateral position (Video 4)
Affords access to the entire lateral aspect of the innominate bone
Does not allow for direct access to the true pelvis; however, access to the anterior column and
the quadrilateral surface can be attained indirectly via the greater sciatic foramen.
Involves the use of a unigastric flip trochanteric osteotomy to avoid release of the gluteus
minimus and medius tendons from the greater trochanter (as originally described)
Commonly used for the following patterns:
Delayed presentation of any acetabular fracture
Transverse
Transverse and posterior wall
T-type
Associated both-column
Involves release of the tensor fascia lata muscle and the entire gluteal muscle group from the
external surface of the ilium, hinging on the superior gluteal neurovascular pedicle

The lateral window of the ilioinguinal approach can be developed via this approach to afford
access to internal iliac fossa; however, this is associated with a risk of devascularizing entire
segments of the ilium and the anterior column and should be avoided if possible.
Video 4 Gorczyca JT, ed: Anterior iliofemoral approach, in Selective Exposures in Orthopaedic
Surgery: The Pelvis [DVD]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2005.
Complications
Heterotopic ossification is the most common complication.21
Abductor muscle detachment or necrosis is prevented via careful dissection/repair and
protection of the superior gluteal artery.22
Abductor muscle dysfunction
Superior gluteal nerve and sciatic nerve can also be injured from prolonged retraction.
Wound dehiscence and infection
Intraoperative Imaging
Standard radiographic views of the acetabulum are obtained intraoperatively and
postoperatively to evaluate fracture reduction and implant placement.

Surgical Fixation
Surgical fixation of acetabular fractures commonly occurs with malleable, small-fragment (3.5
mm) nonlocking (reconstruction-style) plates that can be easily contoured to match the
complex surfaces of the anterior and posterior columns.
Individual screws may be placed outside of the reconstruction plates to compress (lag screw)
or fix (position screw) column fractures or fracture fragments.
Multiple osseous corridors exist within the innominate bone that can accommodate screws of
varying sizes and lengths to stabilize both columns.26
Mini-fragment plates can be used in certain locations around the acetabulum to provisionally
or definitively secure a fracture.27
Pre-contoured implants have been developed for acetabular fracture surgery; however,
surgeons should be cognizant that an anatomic mismatch between the plate and bone may
result in malreduction—particularly at the articular surface.
Currently, pre-contoured plates that support comminuted fractures of the quadrilateral
surface in geriatric or pathologic bone have become increasingly popular.28
Nonsurgical Management
Fractures that are nondisplaced or minimally displaced (<2 mm) may be amenable to
nonsurgical management with limited–weight bearing through the affected extremity for a
period of time (6 to 12 weeks) and close radiographic follow-up.
The presence and maintenance of a congruent hip joint on AP, iliac, and obturator oblique
views is essential for successful nonsurgical management.
Roof-arc measurements have been used to help identify fractures that may be amenable to
nonsurgical management. The roof arc is defined as the angle subtended by a vertical line
from the center of the femoral head and a line from the center of the femoral head to the
location of the fracture within the acetabulum, measured on all three radiographic views of
the acetabulum.29
Roof arcs must be measured in a congruent hip joint.
Roof arc angles less than or equal to 45° on an AP view generally are not amenable to
nonsurgical management.

Roof arc angles do not account for articular displacement.
If necessary, Judet oblique views may help identify subtle instability or subluxation of the
femoral head within the acetabulum.
The literature supports successful nonsurgical management of minimally displaced fractures,
particularly those with articular displacement of less than or equal to 2 mm.30
Secondary congruence describes a condition in which the femoral head remains congruent
with the weight-bearing portion of the acetabulum, even though the entire dome (anterior
column) is displaced. Typically, this condition only occurs with an associated both-column
fracture. Successful nonsurgical management is possible with secondary congruence in frail
geriatric patients or those with severe medical comorbidities precluding surgical
management.31,32
Surgical Management
Surgical reduction and stabilization are indicated in patients with instability or a nonconcentric
relationship of the femoral head with respect to the acetabulum.
Displacement (>2 mm), especially if present in the weight-bearing dome of the acetabulum, is
a relative indication for surgical management.
Surgical treatment does not require a delay and can be performed early, especially for
unstable injuries, as soon as a patient’s condition is stable and optimized.33,34
Outcomes
Literature on the surgical management of acetabular fractures commonly is presented with all
fracture types pooled together or reports the results of a specific surgical approach.
Historically, radiographic outcomes have been the focus of studies on acetabular fracture
management, with quality of reduction consistently showing improved survival of the native
hip.35,36
Multiple survivorship analyses demonstrate that articular step-off (≥1 mm) is tolerated less
well than gap displacement (≥5 mm) in predicting conversion to hip arthroplasty.37
More recently, studies have focused on patient-reported outcomes and long-term outcome
data, with the largest series reporting an overall conversion rate of 20%.1,38,39
Other radiographic predictors of poor outcomes include the following:
Comminuted posterior wall fracture

Impaction of the dome, posterior articular surface, or femoral head
Posterior Wall Fractures
Background
The most common type of acetabular fracture in young, healthy patients
Occur after loading through the femur and commonly are associated with posterior dislocation
of the femoral head, which may result in the following:
Injury to the femoral head blood supply and subsequent osteonecrosis
Articular cartilage lesions or impaction fractures of the femoral head
Marginal impaction of the acetabular articular cartilage
CT scans are obtained after reduction of the dislocation to evaluate for the following:
Impaction of the acetabulum or femoral head
Femoral head fractures
Free intra-articular osteochondral fragments
Although many attempts have been made to correlate the size of the posterior wall fragment
with potential instability, the methodology for calculating percentage size is inaccurate and
fraught with poor predictability and intraobserver reliability.
Recent evidence has shown that wall size less than 20% is not a reliable indicator of stability.40
The superior fracture exit point has been reported to be an important factor in hip stability
after fracture; however, this evidence is not conclusive.41
Dynamic fluoroscopic evaluation of posterior wall fractures can be performed to assess hip
stability if questionable. Hips that are stable on dynamic stress testing have been shown to
result in good short-term outcomes with nonsurgical management.42
Dynamic Stress Examination
Performed under general anesthesia with the patient in the supine position on a radiolucent
table
The fluoroscopic image intensifier is brought in from the ipsilateral side of table, and an
obturator oblique view is obtained (Figure 4).
The examiner places an axial load on the hip throughout this examination.
The ipsilateral hip is brought into flexion and then 20° of adduction and 20° of internal
rotation.

A stable hip remains congruent throughout the examination on all views.

Surgical Management
Posterior wall fractures are commonly managed via a Kocher-Langenbeck approach with the
patient in the lateral or prone position.
A surgical hip dislocation can be performed for combined lesions of the femoral head and the
posterior wall or if characteristics of the injury require greater surgical exposure, such as
extensive marginal impaction.
Entrapped osteochondral or osseous fragments must be removed from within the hip joint
before fixation; this can be accomplished by gently extracting the femoral head from the
acetabulum with the use of a universal distractor. All fragments visualized on the preoperative
CT scans should be accounted for at this time (Figures 5 and 6).

Marginal impaction
Occurs if portions of the posterior acetabular articular surface and the associated
subchondral bone are impacted into the underlying cancellous bone, resulting in a
depression and incongruent joint surface. Occasionally, these may be free osteoarticular
fragments.
Marginal impaction and free articular fragments must be reduced before reduction of the
posterior wall fragments (Figure 7).
These fragments are reduced by using the femoral head as a template, and some form of
structural bone void filler frequently is to help support the reduction.
Figure 7 Axial CT scans of a pelvis with a left comminuted posterior wall fracture. A,
Preoperative CT scan shows marginal impaction. B, Postoperative CT scan shows elevation of
marginal impaction and restoration of the joint surface. (Reproduced from Perdue PW Jr,
Tainter D, Toney C, Lee C: Evaluation and management of posterior wall acetabulum
fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[21]:e1057-e1067.)
Flexible reconstruction plates are used to maintain reduction and buttress posterior wall
fragments, with fixation secured above and below the joint space.
Depending on the size of the posterior wall fragment and the plane of the fracture, small hook
plates, position screws, or lag screws may be used inside or outside the plate.

Postoperative Protocol
Foot-flat–weight bearing for 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively, depending on the fracture pattern,
bone quality, and presence of impaction
Progression to full–weightbearing and normal activities as tolerated are permitted after 6
weeks postoperatively.
Follow-up to evaluate for osteonecrosis of the femoral head or posttraumatic arthritis is based
on surgeon preference or patient symptoms.
Outcomes
Injury characteristics, such as hip dislocation, fracture comminution, intra-articular loose
bodies, concurrent femoral head lesions, and marginal impaction, have been associated with
poor results.1
Patients who undergo surgical fixation of posterior wall fractures have been shown to have
poorer functional outcomes compared with those with other fracture patterns.43
Quality of reduction has been shown to be predictive of radiologic grade, clinical function, and
posttraumatic arthritis.1,44-46
Mark as Complete
